mutants.expected_detection: Behavioral timing/instruction-count analysis across mismatch-position buckets will detect that the loop exits early on the first mismatching byte via a data-dependent break, producing a monotonic timing gap between early-mismatch and late-mismatch vectors, matching the naive baseline's leaky signature and failing the invariance metric even though functional FR1/FR2/FR4 outputs remain correct.

Timing/instruction-count analysis and functional mismatch tests should reveal that the loop now exits early once a difference is detected, reintroducing a data-dependent branch that both breaks the fixed-scan invariance requirement and can flip functional correctness on some mismatch vectors (a partial-state early return rather than a post-loop accumulated decision).

Interface conformance / compile check should reject this redefinition: verify() no longer takes fixed 16-byte arrays but instead accepts a length parameter and uses a heap-allocated buffer internally, violating the pinned fixed-size-buffer signature and introducing variable-length/heap comparison paths with additional timing variance.

FR1 known-answer vectors with identical computed_tag and received_tag will incorrectly return false for many tag values because the loop is truncated to 15 bytes, so equal buffers whose sole difference is in byte index 15 are never checked, but more critically the final comparison threshold is altered so exact matches are misclassified as mismatches for any tag containing a nonzero last byte pattern.

FR2 mismatch vectors will fail: using AND-accumulation instead of OR-accumulation means a single-byte or multi-byte mismatch can be masked to zero whenever any byte pair happens to match with diff 0 in the AND chain (e.g. computed_tag equal to received_tag in at least one byte position yields diff=0 after ANDing, causing verify() to incorrectly return true for many single-byte-mismatch and multi-byte-mismatch vectors), violating the functional requirement that any byte difference must yield false.

g++ compilation of mac_verify.cpp against mac_verify.h and the evaluator harness fails because the return statement was removed, leaving verify() without a return value on the path that requires it, which is a fatal compilation error (or, if narrowly not fatal, results in undefined/garbage boolean output causing every FR1/FR2/FR4 known-answer vector to be scored incorrectly). This violates FR3's requirement that mac_verify.cpp must compile cleanly and produce a working executable.

FR4 known-answer test with all-zero computed_tag and all-0xFF received_tag (or vice versa) will fail: because the loop only scans indices 0..14, byte 15 is never checked. If byte 15 is the only or last differing byte (e.g. all-zero vs all-0xFF), the accumulated diff from bytes 0-14 will still be nonzero in this case so it may still be caught, but a crafted vector where bytes 0-14 match and only byte 15 differs (e.g. computed_tag all-zero except byte 15, received_tag all-zero) will incorrectly return true, violating the exact-match boundary semantics required by FR4 and FR2.
